blocks.text: Real data is missing pieces constantly. A survey respondent skips a question, a sensor drops a reading, a form field was optional and nobody filled it in. Pandas represents all of this with NaN, and knowing how to find it, understand why it behaves strangely, and do something sensible about it is one of the most foundational skills in this whole course.

blocks.alt: An integer column silently upcasting to float the moment a single missing value is introduced
blocks.caption: This single side effect surprises almost everyone the first time they hit it.

blocks.text: 1. What NaN Actually Is

NaN stands for Not a Number, and in pandas it is really a special floating point value inherited straight from NumPy. There is no separate 'missing' type, missing data is represented as a specific float value that behaves oddly on purpose so it can be detected.
1.1 The Integer to Float Upcast Gotcha

Since NaN is a float, a column that was previously a clean int64 gets silently converted to float64 the moment even one missing value shows up in it. Your ages column, which should logically be whole numbers, suddenly displays as 25.0, 30.0, NaN, 40.0.

code.content:
ages = pd.Series([25, 30, 40], dtype="int64")
ages_with_gap = pd.Series([25, 30, None, 40])
print(ages_with_gap.dtype)  # float64, not int64

blocks.title: This is not a bug, it is a real constraint
blocks.content: NumPy's int64 has no way to represent a missing value at all, so pandas has no choice but to upcast to float the moment NaN needs to fit somewhere in that column. The 'Changing Data Types' lesson later in this module covers pandas' nullable Int64 type, which solves exactly this problem.

blocks.text: 2. NaN Behaves Strangely in Comparisons
NaN famously does not equal itself. NaN == NaN evaluates to False, which means you cannot check for missing values using a normal equality comparison the way you would for any other value.

blocks.alt: NaN compared to NaN with the standard equality operator evaluating to False
blocks.caption: This is intentional, by IEEE floating point convention, but it trips up everyone the first time.

code.content: df["col"] == float("nan")  # always False, never actually finds the missing values

blocks.text: Because of this, pandas gives you dedicated functions instead of relying on a comparison.
3. Detecting Missing Values
isna() and isnull() are identical aliases, returning a boolean mask that is True wherever a value is missing. notna() and notnull() are their exact opposites.

blocks.alt: isna producing a boolean mask flagging exactly which positions are missing
blocks.caption: The proper, reliable way to find NaN, unlike an equality comparison.

blocks.text: 3.1 Counting Missing Values Per Column

Chaining .sum() onto isna() gives you a quick per column count, since True counts as 1 and False as 0. This is usually the very first thing you run on a freshly loaded DataFrame, and it is the same information the data-inspection lesson's .info() non-null counts were hinting at, just presented directly as missing counts instead.

blocks.alt: isna summed to give a missing value count for every column at once
blocks.caption: One line, and you know exactly how bad the missing data problem is in each column.

blocks.text: 4. Dropping Missing Data
dropna() removes rows or columns that contain missing values, and its parameters control exactly how aggressive that removal is.

blocks.alt: dropna with axis 0 dropping entire rows versus axis 1 dropping entire columns
blocks.caption: The axis controls what gets removed: whole rows, or whole columns.

code.content:
df.dropna()               # drop rows with any missing value
df.dropna(axis=1)         # drop columns with any missing value

blocks.text: 4.1 Controlling How Strict the Drop Is
how='any', the default, drops a row the moment ANY single value in it is missing. how='all' is much more forgiving, only dropping a row if EVERY value in it is missing.

blocks.alt: dropna with how set to any dropping aggressively versus how set to all dropping only fully empty rows
blocks.caption: any is strict and drops a lot. all only removes rows that are completely empty.

blocks.text: thresh sets a minimum number of non missing values a row must have to survive, giving you finer control than a blunt any versus all choice.

blocks.alt: dropna with thresh requiring at least a certain number of non null values to keep a row
blocks.caption: A middle ground between dropping too aggressively and keeping rows that are mostly empty.

code.content: df.dropna(thresh=3)  # keep rows with at least 3 non null values

blocks.text: 5. Filling Missing Values
fillna() replaces missing values instead of removing the rows that contain them, which matters a lot when dropping would throw away otherwise useful data.

blocks.alt: fillna replacing every missing value in a column with a single constant
blocks.caption: The simplest case: one fill value for every gap.

blocks.text: A dict lets you fill different columns with different values in a single call, which is genuinely how you use this in practice, since different columns almost always need different treatment.

blocks.alt: fillna with a dict specifying a different fill value for each column
blocks.caption: One call, tailored per column fill values.

blocks.text: 5.1 Forward Fill and Backward Fill

ffill carries the last known value forward to fill a gap. bfill carries the next known value backward instead. Neither is universally correct, it depends entirely on whether the previous or next value is actually a reasonable stand in.

blocks.alt: ffill carrying the previous value forward versus bfill carrying the next value backward across a gap
blocks.caption: Genuinely useful for a sensor reading or a stock price. Genuinely wrong for something like a person's age.

blocks.title: ffill and bfill assume continuity that does not always exist
blocks.content: A missing stock price is very likely close to the previous day's price, so ffill makes sense there. A missing age has no relationship to the row before it, so ffill on an ages column would just be wrong. Always ask whether the previous or next value is actually a meaningful default before reaching for ffill or bfill.

blocks.text: 6. Worked Example: A Mixed Strategy
Say you load a messy DataFrame and check its missing pattern first.

code.content:
print(df.isna().sum())
# customer_id      0
# signup_date      0
# age             12
# last_login       8
# plan_tier         3

blocks.text: Different columns call for different treatment. customer_id and signup_date have no missing values, nothing to do there. age is genuinely missing at random, a reasonable default like the median makes sense. last_login is a timestamp where the previous value being close is plausible, so forward fill fits. plan_tier has very few missing values relative to the whole dataset, and there is no sensible default, so dropping just those few rows is cleanest.

code.content:
df["age"] = df["age"].fillna(df["age"].median())
df["last_login"] = df["last_login"].ffill()
df = df.dropna(subset=["plan_tier"])

blocks.alt: A decision flow choosing dropna versus fillna versus ffill based on what each column's values actually represent
blocks.caption: The right strategy depends on the column, not a single blanket rule for the whole DataFrame.

blocks.title: This lesson covers the basics, not deep imputation
blocks.content: This lesson gets you comfortable detecting and doing something reasonable about missing data. A later lesson in this course, Missing Value Imputation, goes much deeper into statistically grounded strategies for filling gaps.

blocks.text: 7. Recap

items: NaN is a special float value, which is why an int column upcasts to float the moment one goes missing.
NaN == NaN is False, so use isna/notna instead of equality checks.
isna().sum() gives a fast per column missing count.
dropna's axis, how, and thresh parameters control how aggressively rows or columns get removed.
fillna handles constants or per column dicts, ffill/bfill only make sense when neighboring values are genuinely meaningful defaults.
